input: The selectivity values that have been reported for the benchmark material by the two groups are, it must be said, remarkably difficult to reconcile with one another, and the size of the disagreement is considerably larger than the scatter that either group reports for its own repeated measurements, which raises important questions about what is really being measured. A closer examination reveals that the difference appears to track the test conditions rather than the material itself. One of the groups derives its values from pure-component isotherms, which are then combined by means of IAST in order to predict what the mixture selectivity ought to be, whereas the other group measures selectivity directly on mixtures, working from the composition of the adsorbed phase that is found in equilibrium with a gas phase of known composition. These two approaches will only deliver the same answer in cases where the adsorbed mixture behaves ideally, and the benchmark material would appear to be one of the cases in which that assumption comes under considerable strain, since the components involved differ markedly in the strength with which they interact with the surface and indeed with one another. It is also worth noting that, where the isotherm route is followed, the resulting prediction inevitably inherits any weaknesses in the fitting of the pure-component data at low pressure, which is a region in which the two groups did not measure with equal care. On balance, therefore, the mixture measurements are to be preferred for the benchmark material, although this preference is subject to an important condition, namely that it holds where the comparison is made at feed compositions and total pressures that are reasonably close to those of the intended separation, and it ceases to hold in situations where the mixture data were obtained far away from those conditions.
target: The selectivity values reported for the benchmark material by the two groups do not agree, and the disagreement is larger than the scatter each group reports for repeated measurements of its own. The difference follows the test conditions rather than the material. One group obtains its values from pure-component isotherms, combined through IAST into a predicted mixture selectivity; the other measures selectivity directly on mixtures, from the composition of the adsorbed phase in equilibrium with a gas phase of known composition. The two quantities coincide only where the adsorbed mixture behaves ideally. For the benchmark material that assumption is strained, because the components differ in how strongly they interact with the surface and with each other. The isotherm route also imports the fit of the pure-component data at low pressure, a region in which the two groups measured with different care, so part of the gap between the reported values is a gap in the underlying data rather than in the material. The mixture measurements are therefore preferred for the benchmark material, on one condition: the preference holds where the comparison is made at feed compositions and total pressures close to those of the intended separation, and it lapses where the mixture data were taken far from those conditions. Judged on that basis, the higher of the two reported values rests on the isotherm route and is set aside, and the lower value, measured on mixtures, is the value carried forward for this material class.
